html:
The Wall Street crash was the collapse of share prices on the New York Stock Exchange in October 1929. It opened the Great Depression, the worst economic slump of the industrial age.

The 1920s had been a boom in the United States. Cars like the Model T, radios and electric goods sold fast, and share prices rose year after year. Many people bought shares with borrowed money, putting down as little as a tenth of the price. By 1929 prices had risen far above what companies earned.

The fall came in waves. On "Black Thursday", 24 October, panic selling set a record of nearly 13 million shares traded; bankers bought shares to calm the market. On "Black Tuesday", 29 October, the panic returned with over 16 million shares sold. Buyers who had borrowed had to sell to repay loans, which drove prices lower still. By 1932 the market had lost almost 90 percent of its value from the 1929 peak.

The crash alone did not cause the Depression, but it destroyed confidence. Thousands of American banks failed, credit dried up, and unemployment rose to about a quarter of workers. Because American loans had propped up Europe after the First World War, the slump spread worldwide, and countries put up tariffs that shrank trade further. The suffering helped bring Franklin D. Roosevelt and the New Deal to power in the US, and helped extremist parties win elsewhere, above all the Nazis in Germany. After the Second World War, Bretton Woods tried to make sure it would not happen again.
sum: The Wall Street crash was the collapse of share prices on the New York Stock Exchange in October 1929. It opened the Great Depression, the worst economic slump of the industrial age.
